14:5.text: I shall see him, but not now: I shall behold him, but not nigh: there shall come a Star out of Jacob, and a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel, and shall smite the corners of Moab, and destroy all the children of Sheth.

provenance.other: The Book of Mormon's 'a new star' is in no KJV verse; the King James Bible's messianic star is Balaam's ('there shall come a Star out of Jacob') and the magi's ('we have seen his star in the east').
provenance.significance: The figure, not the wording. The King James Bible has exactly one prophet who is not of Israel, is hired to curse Israel, and prophesies a star at Israel's redemption instead — and Samuel the Lamanite is standing on the wall of a Nephite city in that position. Recovering Balaam gives the sign its shape: the star is announced by the outsider, and the insiders resent the announcement. Matthew 2:2 completes the circuit by having Gentile astrologers, not Jerusalem, see the star when it comes.

14:5.note: Offered as a typology and not as a borrowing. There is no verbal contact — 'a new star' is not KJV English — and the link is entirely in the speaker's position: the KJV's star prophecies belong to a foreign seer (Numbers 24:17) and to foreign magi (Matthew 2:2), and Samuel is a Lamanite. Recorded at low confidence because the reading is worth having in front of a reader and cannot be argued from the words.
14:5.whyNot: No shared wording at all. A reader who thinks a nativity star needs no source beyond the nativity is entitled to decline this, and the catalogue is not claiming the writer had Balaam in view.

14:6.text: He delivereth and rescueth, and he worketh signs and wonders in heaven and in earth, who hath delivered Daniel from the power of the lions.

provenance.other: “Signs and wonders in heaven” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Daniel 6:27. The bare phrase 'signs and wonders' occurs in fourteen and is almost always Egypt or the apostles; only Daniel puts the wonders in heaven. Acts 2:19, quoting Joel 2:30, has 'wonders in heaven above, and signs in the earth beneath', which divides the pair between the two realms instead of putting both aloft.
provenance.significance: The one KJV verse that locates signs and wonders in heaven is spoken by Darius the Mede — a foreign king issuing a decree about the God of a captive minority. Samuel is the mirror image: a member of the despised nation telling the ruling one what its God will do in its sky. In Daniel the confession follows the deliverance; here it precedes the sign, which is the whole difficulty the sermon runs into.

14:6.note: 'There shall be many signs and wonders in Heaven.' 'Signs and wonders in heaven' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Moderate rather than high because 'signs and wonders' is one of the KJV's commonest formulas and the Book of Mormon uses it freely elsewhere, so the localisation in heaven is the only distinctive element. Note that the fuller Joel/Acts form, which divides signs and wonders between heaven and earth, is the one the chapter's later verses actually enact (14:21-22 puts the shaking 'both above the earth and beneath'), so it is registered as a composite rather than passed over.

14:8.text: He that believeth on the Son hath everlasting life: and he that believeth not the Son shall not see life; but the wrath of God abideth on him.

provenance.other: “Believeth on the Son” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 3:36 and 1 John 5:10; John 3:36 is the only one that completes it with 'hath everlasting life', and 1 John 5:10 is the only one that reads 'believeth on the Son of God', which is the Book of Mormon's fuller phrase.
provenance.significance: The verse is the Johannine formula assembled from its two KJV halves. Recovering John 3:36 supplies the clause the Book of Mormon leaves out and its whole sermon depends on — 'he that believeth not the Son shall not see life; but the wrath of God abideth on him' — which is what chapters 15 and 16 are about. Samuel gives his audience the promise and lets the threat stand behind it; John states both.

14:8.note: 'Whosoever shall believe on the Son of God, the same shall have everlasting life.' 'Believeth on the Son' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, and the Book of Mormon has 1 John 5:10's fuller subject with John 3:36's predicate. John 3:16's 'whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life' is the better-known verse and reads 'in him' rather than 'on the Son'. Moderate: this is Johannine boilerplate that the Book of Mormon uses continually, so what is being catalogued is the source of the formula rather than a fresh act of borrowing at this verse.

14:9.text: The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the LORD, make straight in the desert a highway for our God.

provenance.route: Isaiah 40:3 → Matthew 3:2-3 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Prepare ye the way of the Lord” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Isaiah 40:3 and its three synoptic citations — and the wording is identical in all four, so the phrase alone cannot decide mediation and tools/mediation-check.py returns no decisive divergence for this verse. What decides it is the pairing with repentance, which is not in Isaiah: 'Repent ye' is Matthew 3:2, one verse before the citation.
provenance.significance: Samuel is given the Baptist's commission verbatim, and he is given it by an angel. Recover Matthew 3 and the identification is not a flourish but a structure: the herald cries in a wilderness outside the city, preaches repentance, threatens the axe at the root of the tree — and Helaman 14:18 supplies that axe's sentence nine verses later. What the Book of Mormon adds is the audience's reply, which Matthew reports as coming from the Pharisees and Samuel has already received in chapter 13.

14:9.note: 'He hath said unto me, Cry unto this people, repent and prepare the way of the Lord.' Three elements of Isaiah 40:3 as the gospels use it — the cry, the repentance, the preparing of the way. mediation-check.py finds no decisive divergence between Isaiah 40:3 and Matthew 3:3, because the KJV renders the quoted clause identically in both; the mediation is argued from elsewhere, as CONVENTIONS §7 allows. Two things carry it. 'Repent' belongs to Matthew 3:2 and not to Isaiah 40, where the crier says 'All flesh is grass'. And the sermon quotes the Baptist's preaching again at 14:18, where 'hewn down, and cast into the fire' is reproduced word for word. One Isaiah 40 citation could be either; a citation plus the Baptist's threat is the gospel setting.

14:15.text: And said unto them, Thus it is written, and thus it behoved Christ to suffer, and to rise from the dead the third day:

provenance.other: “Behoved” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Luke 24:46 and Hebrews 2:17, and only Luke's attaches it to Christ suffering and rising. “It is expedient” occurs in exactly two, John 11:50 and John 16:7, and only John 11:50 attaches it to a death.
provenance.significance: Two KJV rarities from two different necessities, fused. Luke 24:46 is the risen Christ on the road telling two disciples what had to happen; John 11:50 is Caiaphas telling a council why a man had to die. The Book of Mormon puts them in one clause — 'it behooveth him, and becometh expedient that he dieth' — so that the divine necessity and the political calculation say the same sentence. That is the same fusion 1 Nephi 4:13 made when Nephi justified killing Laban in Caiaphas's words; here the borrowing has come back to its proper object, and the expediency that was frightening in Nephi's mouth is orthodox in Samuel's.

14:15.note: 'He surely must die, that salvation may come; yea, it behooveth him, and becometh expedient that he dieth, to bring to pass the resurrection of the dead.' Against Luke 24:46: 'thus it behoved Christ to suffer, and to rise from the dead the third day.' 'Behoved' occurs in exactly two KJV verses and Luke's is the only christological one; the resurrection follows in both, and 14:20's 'for the space of three days, to the time that he shall rise again from the dead' supplies Luke's third day. The second rare word is 'expedient', which the KJV joins to a death in exactly one verse, John 11:50 — see the argument at 1 Nephi 4:13, where the same verse is borrowed to justify a killing.

14:18.text: And now also the axe is laid unto the root of the trees: therefore every tree which bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire.

provenance.other: “Hewn down and cast into the fire” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Matthew 3:10, Matthew 7:19 and Luke 3:9. The clause is word-identical in all three, so it cannot itself choose between them; Matthew 3:10 and Luke 3:9 are the Baptist's preaching and Matthew 7:19 is the Sermon on the Mount.
provenance.significance: The Baptist's axe, transplanted from a tree to a person. In all three KJV verses the thing hewn down is a tree that does not bear good fruit — a figure — and the Book of Mormon drops the figure and applies the sentence directly to 'whosoever repenteth not'. Recovering the source restores what the Book of Mormon has taken out: the axe already laid to the root, which is to say the interval before the blow, which is exactly the interval Samuel says his audience is standing in.

14:18.note: 'Whosoever repenteth, the same is not hewn down and cast into the fire; but whosoever repenteth not, is hewn down and cast into the fire.' A six-word clause reproduced twice in one sentence, occurring in exactly three KJV verses. Which of the three cannot be settled on the wording, since the clause is identical in all; Matthew 3:10 is preferred because 14:9 has already given Samuel the Baptist's commission from Matthew 3:2-3, so the sermon is working in that chapter. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his quotations; catalogued as a quotation on the §2 rule.

14:18.text: But the fearful, and unbelieving, and the abominable, and murderers, and whoremongers, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, shall have their part in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone: which is the second death.

provenance.other: “The second death” occurs in exactly four KJV verses, Revelation 2:11, 20:6, 20:14 and 21:8, and nowhere else in the Bible. Revelation 21:8 is the only one that defines it by what precedes — the lake which burneth with fire — which is the image the same Book of Mormon verse has just used.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon takes John's term and gives it a definition John does not: a second cutting off from the presence of the Lord 'as to things pertaining to righteousness'. Recovering Revelation shows what has been changed. There the second death is a place, the lake of fire; here it is a relation, and the fire from the Baptist's axe in the first half of the verse has been left to carry the imagery. The two halves of Helaman 14:18 are two different apocalypses spliced at the word 'fire'.

14:18.note: 'There cometh upon them again a spiritual death, yea, a second death.' The phrase belongs to Revelation and to no other biblical book — exactly four KJV verses — and the surrounding image of being cast into fire is Revelation 20:14 and 21:8's. Moderate because 'second death' had become a standing term in the Book of Mormon's own theological vocabulary by this point (compare Alma 12-13) and may be arriving from there rather than freshly from John; what argues for the KJV here is the immediate juxtaposition with the fire.

14:20.text: But in those days, after that tribulation, the sun shall be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light,

provenance.route: Isaiah 13:10 → Mark 13:24-25 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “The sun shall be darkened” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 13:10 and Mark 13:24 — the second quoting the first. tools/mediation-check.py returns two decisive points, both for Mark: the Book of Mormon has neither Isaiah's 'in his going forth' nor Isaiah's 'to shine' (backbone of four further shared words — sun, darkened, moon, light).
provenance.significance: The order settles what the tool measures. Isaiah 13:10 runs stars, sun, moon; Mark 13:24-25 runs sun, moon, stars; Helaman 14:20 runs 'the sun shall be darkened … and also the moon, and the stars', which is the gospel sequence. And the setting has moved: Isaiah darkens the sun for the fall of Babylon and Mark for the end of the age, while the Book of Mormon does it for a single execution — the Olivet apocalypse relocated from the last day to Good Friday, which is where Luke 23:44-45 had already put a smaller version of it.

14:20.note: 'The sun shall be darkened and refuse to give his light unto you; and also the moon, and the stars.' The clause occurs in exactly two KJV verses, and the mediation test is decisive for the New Testament form: mediation-check.py finds the Book of Mormon has dropped both of Isaiah 13:10's distinctive additions ('in his going forth', 'to shine'), and the sun-moon-stars order is Mark's and Matthew's rather than Isaiah's. Matthew 24:29 has the same sequence but reads 'shall the sun be darkened'; the Book of Mormon has Mark's word order exactly. What the Book of Mormon supplies on its own is the duration, three days, and the second-person 'unto you'.

14:21.text: And, behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom; and the earth did quake, and the rocks rent;

provenance.other: “The rocks rent” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 27:51. “Rent in twain” occurs in exactly two, Matthew 27:51 and Mark 15:38, both of the temple veil. “Yielded up the ghost” occurs in three, of which Matthew 27:50 is the only one of Christ.
provenance.significance: Everything in Matthew's sentence is transferred to the Book of Mormon's landscape except the veil. Matthew has the veil rent in twain, the earth quaking, the rocks rending; Helaman 14:21-22 has the earth shaking, the rocks broken up, and — the giveaway — the rocks 'rent in twain', which in the KJV is what happens to the veil and not to the rocks. The suppressed correspondence is the temple itself: a land with no temple veil to tear gets the tearing anyway, in the veil's own words, written across its geology. The seams and cracks are said to remain 'ever after', so the sign is permanent where Matthew's was momentary.

14:21.note: 'At the time that he shall yield up the ghost … the earth shall shake and tremble, and the rocks … shall be broken up; yea, they shall be rent in twain.' Three phrases from two consecutive KJV verses: 'yielded up the ghost' (Matthew 27:50, the only christological one of three), 'the rocks rent' (a KJV singleton at Matthew 27:51) and 'rent in twain' (exactly two verses, both the temple veil). The Book of Mormon has swapped the last of these from the veil onto the rocks, which is the strongest evidence in the passage that Matthew 27:51 is being read rather than merely paralleled.

14:23.text: Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low: and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough places plain:

provenance.other: tools/mediation-check.py reports one decisive point favouring Isaiah 40:4 over Luke 3:5 — 'places plain' against 'ways shall be made smooth' — but the match is on the word 'places', which in Helaman 14:23 belongs to 'many places, which are now called valleys' and has nothing to do with Isaiah's rough places. The reported backbone (valley, mountain, hill, low, crooked, straight, rough) is shared between the two candidates and not with the Book of Mormon, which has only valley, mountain and low. The tool's verdict is set aside here on inspection; the mediation is recorded as direct-OT on the strength of 14:9, not on this diff.
provenance.significance: Fourteen verses after quoting Isaiah 40:3, the sermon makes Isaiah 40:4 happen. In Isaiah the levelling of the land is a metaphor for clearing a processional road; here mountains are laid low and valleys thrown up as literal seismic damage at the death of the one whose way was being prepared. That is metalepsis running in an unusual direction — the source's figure is recovered and then cashed as an event, so the highway prepared in verse 9 is built by the earthquake in verse 23.

14:23.note: 'There shall be many mountains laid low, like unto a valley, and there shall be many places, which are now called valleys, which shall become mountains.' Isaiah 40:4's 'every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low' is the only KJV verse that exchanges valleys and mountains, and the sermon has already cited the verse before it at 14:9. Moderate: the wording is a paraphrase ('laid low' is in no KJV verse; “made low” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Isaiah 2:17, Isaiah 40:4 and James 1:10), and an earthquake that flattens hills needs no source. What raises it above coincidence is the pairing with 14:9 in one speech.

14:25.text: And the graves were opened; and many bodies of the saints which slept arose,

provenance.other: “The graves were opened” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 27:52. “Appeared unto many” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 27:53. They are consecutive verses, and Helaman 14:25 reproduces both in Matthew's order in a single sentence of nineteen words.
provenance.significance: Two KJV singletons from two consecutive verses is as strong as the evidence in this catalogue gets, and what it discloses is a choice. Matthew 27:52-53 is the strangest half-sentence in the passion narrative — bodies of saints raised, waiting three days, and walking into the holy city — and it is precisely that episode, not the veil, the darkness or the centurion's confession, that the Book of Mormon promises will be repeated in the New World. Recovering Matthew supplies the detail Samuel leaves out and 3 Nephi will need: the saints appear 'after his resurrection', which is why 14:20's darkness has to last three days.

14:25.note: 'And many graves shall be opened, and shall yield up many of their dead; and many saints shall appear unto many.' Against Matthew 27:52-53: 'And the graves were opened; and many bodies of the saints which slept arose, And came out of the graves after his resurrection … and appeared unto many.' Both distinctive phrases are KJV singletons and both belong to this one pair of verses; the shared noun 'saints' and the repeated 'many' do the rest. The Book of Mormon's one addition is 'yield up … their dead', which is Revelation 20:13's idiom for the sea and death. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his quotations; catalogued as a quotation on the §2 rule.

14:27.text: And Moses stretched forth his hand toward heaven; and there was a thick darkness in all the land of Egypt three days:

provenance.other: “Thick darkness” occurs in exactly 9 KJV verses, most of them Sinai theophany. Exodus 10:22 is the only KJV verse that gives a darkness a duration of three days, and the number is the whole of the contact here.
provenance.significance: The ninth plague is the KJV's one three-day darkness, and it is a plague on Egypt from which Israel is exempt — 'all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings' (Exodus 10:23). Helaman 14:27 has darkness covering 'the face of the whole earth' with no exemption stated, and 3 Nephi will report that there was none. Recovering Exodus makes the difference audible: this is the plague without the Goshen.

14:27.note: 'Darkness should cover the face of the whole earth, for the space of three days.' The synoptic darkness at the crucifixion lasts three hours (Matthew 27:45), not three days; the only three-day darkness in the King James Bible is the ninth plague. Moderate and conceptual: the shared material is a number and a condition rather than wording, and the sign is announced twice in this chapter (14:20, 14:27) in the Book of Mormon's own phrasing. Filed because a reader tracing the three days will otherwise find only the gospels, where they are the days in the tomb, not days of darkness.

14:28.text: Jesus answered and said unto him, Because I said unto thee, I saw thee under the fig tree, believest thou? thou shalt see greater things than these.

provenance.other: “Greater things than these” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 1:50, and in that verse it is a promise made to a man who has just believed on the strength of a smaller sign.
provenance.significance: John 1:50-51 is the KJV's model of the sign that escalates: Nathanael believes because Jesus saw him under a fig tree, and is told he will see greater things — heaven open, the angels ascending and descending. Helaman 14:28 makes the same promise to a crowd that has not believed at all, which reverses the condition. In John the greater things are the reward of faith; here they are given 'to the intent that there should be no cause for unbelief', and chapter 16 records that they produced it anyway.

14:28.note: 'The angel said unto me that many shall see greater things than these, to the intent that they might believe.' 'Greater things than these' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and that verse joins the phrase to believing, as this one does. Moderate: four words, and they are ordinary enough that a writer could assemble them without John. What argues for the borrowing is that the KJV uses this exact comparative once, and uses it for the same transaction — signs offered as grounds for belief.

14:31.text: I call heaven and earth to record this day against you, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life, that both thou and thy seed may live:

provenance.other: “Choose life” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 30:19, which is also the KJV's one verse setting life and death before a people as an object of choice. Deuteronomy 30:15 supplies the other pair the Book of Mormon uses: 'life and good, and death and evil'.
provenance.significance: Samuel ends his doctrinal section where Moses ends his covenant, and the two Deuteronomy verses supply both halves of the Book of Mormon's sentence in Moses's own order — good and evil first (30:15), life and death second (30:19). The suppressed clause is the one Moses adds and Samuel does not: 'that both thou and thy seed may live'. The whole sermon is about whether the seed will live, and chapter 15 answers that for the Lamanites and 15:17 for the Nephites.

14:31.note: 'He hath given unto you that ye might know good from evil, and he hath given unto you that ye might choose life or death.' The two pairs are Deuteronomy 30:15's ('life and good, and death and evil') and 30:19's ('life and death … therefore choose life'), and 'choose life' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. What the Book of Mormon adds is the ground of the choice — 'ye are free; ye are permitted to act for yourselves' at 14:30 — which turns Moses's exhortation into an argument about agency. Compare 13:29's 'how long will ye choose darkness rather than light', where the same verb is already doing this work.
